Alastor, who had stayed silent until then, was carefully watching the shapes drifting above them, his eyes narrowed in concentration. — Maybe we shouldn't try to see, he said slowly. Maybe we should try to feel. Something like 81, with all the power he's absorbed, can't just be floating in the void like everything else. It must... weigh on this place, one way or another. Takeshi, still unsettled by the vastness of the place, ventured to speak up. — Weigh how? he asked. Like, physically? — Like gravity, Alastor answered. If this place keeps everything that's been forgotten, then a being as enormous as him must create some kind of point of attraction. We just need to find the direction where everything seems to... converge. Isidora froze for a moment, a slow smile stretching across her lips. — That, she said, is the first intelligent idea you've had since we left, Al. I'm almost proud of you. — Almost, Alastor repeated with an ironic smile. Lucifer closed his eyes for a moment, a focused expression crossing his face, before opening them again and slowly pointing in a direction in the darkness — a point that, at first glance, was in no way different from the rest of the surrounding void. — There, he said. I feel something, that way. A heaviness. Like a debt that hasn't been fully paid. The group turned toward the indicated direction, the water lapping gently around their feet as a heavy silence settled, each of them aware that the next step they took would bring them, one way or another, closer to the most dangerous being ever recorded in the two Codices. Isidora suddenly froze, a smile lighting up her face as if a light bulb had just switched on above her head. — Oh fuck, I know! she exclaimed. We just have to ask the magic chair! A confused silence greeted this declaration, every eye turning to her. — The what? asked Lucifer, one eyebrow raised so high it threatened to disappear into his hair. — The Answer, Isidora clarified, as if it were the most obvious thing in the world. That omniscient entity stashed somewhere in this dimension, that answers every question except two. It's supposed to be here, right? That's exactly what we need! Alastor frowned, a new caution crossing his eyes. — You sure that's a good idea? he said. Every soul only gets three questions in its entire existence. And if you ask a forbidden question — like how to defeat KJ or Grand Patron Luigi — it self-destructs on the spot. — Well, that's exactly why we'll be careful, Isidora answered with a shrug. We just ask where 81 is. It's not exactly a trick question. Takeshi, who had followed the exchange with growing apprehension, raised a hesitant hand. — Wait, he said, but how do we find her? Nobody's ever managed to reach her, have they? — No known method, Isidora confirmed, a predatory smile reappearing on her lips. But hey, we're already in a dimension that's supposed to be impossible to enter. So we might as well give it a shot. Lucifer sighed long and hard, running a hand over his face. — Great, he said. Yet another plan that relies entirely on total improvisation. — Got a better idea? Isidora shot back. The silence that followed was her only answer. They walked in silence across the liquid expanse, the water lapping faintly around their steps, while above them shapes kept drifting through the darkness — some resembling broken objects, others fragments of words, sometimes entire sentences, vanishing as soon as they seemed to take shape. — Look, Lulu, it's full of bullshit, kind of like your big dickhead skull, Isidora called out, pointing at a shapeless mass floating lazily above them. — Your humor is always a pleasure, Lucifer answered without even looking up. They kept going, the atmosphere gradually growing denser, heavier, as if the air itself — if it could still be called that here — were slowly tightening around them. Then, in the distance, a strange silhouette began to take shape: a heap of furniture, dozens, maybe hundreds of pieces, piled on top of each other, floating a few meters above the liquid ground — chairs, tables, wardrobes, some familiar, others in a style Takeshi had never seen. — What's all this crap? asked Lucifer, slowing down. Isidora had stopped dead, her eyes fixed on the pile of furniture with a new, almost religious intensity. — It's here, she said simply. — How can you be so sure? asked Alastor, one eyebrow raised. It's literally a pile of forgotten furniture. It could be anything. Isidora didn't answer right away, her eyes still riveted on the floating heap, something in her attitude having completely changed — no more sarcasm, no more nonchalance, just a quiet, inexplicable certainty. — I don't know how to explain it to you, Al, she said finally, her voice lower than usual. But I feel it. Like something pulling at the back of my skull. It's here. The chair is here. Takeshi, uncomfortable with this sudden change of tone in her, moved a little closer to the group. — And how do we find it in there? he asked, gesturing at the chaotic pile of suspended furniture. Isidora took a deep breath and stepped toward the floating heap, the water lapping gently around her feet. — We search, she answered simply. And we pray it isn't the wrong chair. They spread out among the heap, methodically searching through dozens of suspended pieces of furniture, pushing aside ordinary chairs, busted armchairs, wobbly tables — until Alastor, pulling on a half-collapsed chest of drawers, uncovered, nestled behind a stack of wardrobes, a chair decidedly different from all the others. Its wood seemed both ancient and intact, without a trace of wear or dust, and on top of its backrest sat a small crystal sphere, translucent, inside which a faint, almost hypnotic glow was dancing. — That's her, Isidora breathed, rushing forward. She took hold of it with a care unusual for her, carrying it at arm's length to a clearer patch of the liquid ground, where she set it down delicately, then stepped back a few paces, as if the object might shatter at the slightest sudden movement. A tense silence settled, every eye fixed on the empty chair, no one daring to make the first move. — Well, Lucifer said finally, who asks the first question? — Not me, Isidora answered immediately, stepping back even further. I already used my three questions centuries ago. I'm not allowed anymore. Every eye then turned to Alastor, who immediately raised his hands in refusal. — Oh no, count me out, he said. If I ask a lousy question and this thing blows up before we get the answer we want, I don't want it to be my fault. Lucifer sighed, glancing resignedly at the sphere. — And if I'm the one asking, and I make a mistake, he said, it's the king of Hell himself who burns a question. A bit more symbolic weight, isn't it? Every eye inevitably ended up converging on Takeshi, who felt his stomach knot all at once. — Wait, no, he said, backing away instinctively. Why me? — You've never asked anybody a question, Isidora answered with a shrug. You've still got your three chances intact. And incidentally, it's kind of your father and your Poppy problem that got us all the way here, so... — So what? Takeshi insisted, panic clearly showing in his voice. — So it's kind of logical that you're the one who asks, Alastor concluded with a smile that was anything but reassuring. Takeshi stood frozen for a moment, his eyes moving from the empty chair to the faces around him, all silent, all waiting. Then, with an almost painful slowness, he stepped toward the crystal sphere, his voice hesitant when he finally broke the silence. — And... and what do I ask first? Where 81 is, or where my father is? A voice suddenly rang out, calm, composed, coming from no visible mouth — seeming to emanate directly from the crystal sphere resting on the chair's backrest, vibrating in the air with a clarity strangely at odds with the heavy silence of the surrounding dimension. — Hello, visitors, said the voice. So, you managed to come here. Not everyone can. But I believe I recognize Isidora, who came here several centuries ago. Isidora stiffened slightly, a tense smile replacing her usual confidence. — Yeah, it's been a while, she answered, her voice losing a little of its customary composure. — But for the others, the voice went on, let me introduce myself. I am The Answer. A silence settled, everyone holding their breath before this invisible entity that nevertheless seemed to be watching them all, with a precision that gave them goosebumps. Takeshi, still motionless in front of the chair, felt his throat tighten even more. — Do you... do you know why we're here? he asked, his voice trembling. — I know everything there is to know, The Answer replied, in a perfectly neutral tone, neither warm nor cold. But I only answer questions asked directly. So, young Mystic — for that is indeed what you are, isn't it — ask your question. Just remember: three questions per soul, not one more. And two questions in particular will cause my immediate destruction if you ask them. Think carefully. Takeshi took a deep breath, his hands trembling slightly as he stared at the crystal sphere. — How do we free 81, oh great omniscient chair? — Could you please stop sucking up to it, Isidora called from the back, a sardonic smile on her lips despite the tension in the air. A silence followed, longer than the previous one, as if The Answer were taking the time to weigh each word before replying. — This crystal sphere resting on me is not something that belongs to me, it said finally, its voice as neutral as ever. It was placed there. And I do believe that a soul has been training for a long time, here, in this dimension. The group exchanged confused looks, Lucifer frowning first. — Wait, he said, are you telling us someone else is already here? For how long? — I do not have the answer to that precise question, The Answer replied. But the energy of this sphere does not come from me. It was placed deliberately, by a consciousness present in this dimension, capable of interacting with my structure without directly summoning me. Takeshi felt his heart race, a lightning-fast thought crossing his mind. — My father, he murmured. Could it be my father? — I can neither confirm nor deny that hypothesis unless you ask the question formally, The Answer replied. Remember: your first question — how to free 81 — remains pending. Do you wish me to answer it, or would you rather rephrase it to ask instead about the identity of this presence? Isidora stepped forward, a new urgency in her voice. — Wait, kid, think carefully, she said. You've only got three questions. If you change your mind now, it doesn't count as used, but if you phrase it badly, you might lose your chance for good. Takeshi clenched his fists, his decision made. — Yes, I want to know where 81 is, he said, his voice firm despite the trembling still in his hands. A silence settled, heavier than the previous ones, before The Answer spoke again, its voice as neutral as ever but charged with a new weight. — This crystal sphere, it said, is the God Killer's prison. A stunned silence fell over the entire group. Takeshi took a step back, his gaze settling with growing horror on the small translucent sphere that had been resting just above his head from the start, that faint glow dancing peacefully inside it. — Wait, said Lucifer, his voice strangled. Are you telling us that 81 — THE 81, the one who destroyed Heaven, who devoured a billion years of gods — is stashed away in this little thing the size of a golf ball? — The physical size of a container has no bearing on the power or the entity it holds, The Answer replied. A consciousness as vast as 81's was compressed, fragment by fragment, into this enclosed space, by the ten beings responsible for his sealing. It is not an ordinary prison. It is a prison on the scale of his soul. Isidora had frozen, her eyes riveted on the sphere with a new intensity, a mixture of fascination and pure terror crossing her usually so offhand features. — And that famous consciousness that's been "training" here for a while, she said slowly, you're telling me it might be the one that put this chair here. On purpose. Right next to 81's prison. — That is a possibility I can neither confirm nor deny without a direct question, The Answer repeated. Takeshi, still in shock, looked up at the sphere he had almost literally been holding in his hands a few moments earlier without knowing it, a chilling thought gradually forcing itself on him. — He said it had to be put somewhere else, he murmured, turning to Isidora. You moved that chair yourself, with that thing on it. We... we literally carried his prison without knowing it. Takeshi hesitated a split second before asking his second question, his voice more confident than before. — How can we free him? — To free 81, The Answer replied without the slightest delay, you just need to take this crystal sphere and break it, by throwing it on the ground, for example. But I advise you to do so on physical ground. A stunned silence greeted this answer of almost comical simplicity, in total contrast with the cosmic scale of the entity in question. — This is a joke, said Lucifer, his voice incredulous. Like, we've got ten super-powerful beings — including an Incarnation of Death and five Archdragons — who joined forces to seal away the most dangerous threat ever known... and all it takes is dropping it on the floor to screw everything up? — The complexity of a seal does not necessarily lie in the fragility of its breaking point, The Answer replied, but in the difficulty of reaching it. No one before you had located this dimension, let alone this specific sphere. The simplicity of the final act in no way diminishes the difficulty of the road traveled to get there. Isidora was already backing away instinctively, her hands raised as if to push Takeshi away from the sphere he was still holding between his fingers. — Wait, wait, wait, she said hastily. Put that fucking ball down right now, kid. Like, right now, right now. Takeshi looked down at the sphere he hadn't even noticed he had picked up again, a cold sweat instantly running down his spine. — Wait, he said, his voice going up a notch, you were telling me that while I was holding it in my hands?! — Technically, The Answer specified, as long as it is not broken on a surface dense enough to release the pressure contained inside, it remains stable. You were safe. Probably. — "Probably"?! Takeshi repeated, panic completely overwhelming him as he knelt with exaggerated slowness to set the sphere back down on the liquid ground with the delicacy of a bomb technician defusing a bomb. Takeshi, still shaken, slowly straightened up, taking a trembling breath before asking his last question. — Where is my father? — Your father is... IN THAILAND! Isidora yelled, cutting off the voice that was starting to answer. — I will start again, The Answer said in a perfectly even tone, as if the interruption had never even happened. — So your father is... AN ASSHOLE! Isidora shouted again, grinning from ear to ear. — I will start again, The Answer repeated, unruffled. — Your father... ABANDONED YOU! Isidora bellowed once more, punctuating every word with a theatrical sweep of her arm. — SHUT UP! I WANT TO TALK! The Answer finally shouted, its voice losing every trace of neutrality for the first time since their arrival. — SO I'M STARTING AGAAAAAIN! The Answer yelled over Isidora, visibly delighted by the chaos it was causing. YOUR FATHER IS LOCKED UP IN THE CULT OF... XAVIER DUPONT DE LIGONNÈS! — WILL YOU SHUT YOUR MOUTH!!! The Answer retorted, the crystal sphere vibrating violently under the sudden intensity of its voice, an irritated light pulsing inside it. A shocked silence abruptly fell again, Lucifer and Alastor doubled over, unable to hold back their laughter, while Takeshi stood open-mouthed, torn between hilarity and total dismay. — Your father, The Answer finally went on, its voice gradually regaining its usual calm, though still tinged with perceptible annoyance, is being held by the Cult of KJ. He is still alive. Takeshi froze, the words taking several seconds to truly sink into his mind, every trace of amusement evaporating instantly. — He... he's alive, he murmured, his voice trembling. Are you sure? — I am never wrong, The Answer replied. Your father is being held somewhere within the Cult of KJ, since the War of the Estrangement. That was your last question. You have now used your three questions. I can no longer answer any other, for this life. Isidora, a smile still hanging on her lips, crossed her arms with perfect nonchalance. — Then again, it's true he could've been in Thailand, getting his ass kneaded by some Thai girl, huh. We don't know. We don't judge. A brief silence preceded The Answer's reply, its voice returning to an icy calm, almost threatening in its recovered neutrality. — Isidora, it said, if I had arms, legs, charisma, strength, solidity — and not just someone else's prison to show off with — I would come and knead that bitch skull of yours. A stunned silence greeted this retort, before Lucifer burst out laughing once again, even louder than before, almost doubling over. — Now that, he said between hiccups, is the best thing I've heard in centuries. An ancient omniscient entity threatening to knead Isidora's skull. Isidora, for her part, stayed open-mouthed for a moment, before a delighted smile spread across her face, visibly more impressed than insulted. — Okay, she said, respect. I didn't think you had that in you, chair. — I am not a chair, The Answer replied curtly. I am an omniscient consciousness forced to reside in a piece of furniture for lack of options. There is a difference. — Yeah, yeah, said Isidora, waving a casual hand, the chair. Well, thanks for the info, anyway. Even if you nearly fried twice because of me. Takeshi, still shaken by the revelation about his father, stayed silent, his gaze lost in the dark immensity of the dimension, a new and fragile determination slowly beginning to form behind the persistent worry that filled him.

qualdi-t1-c1.title: Chapter 1 — Getting Down to Business
qualdi-t1-c1.html:
Bullets whistled down the alley.

Two members of the Chimamire clan were running flat out, a Toride squad right on their heels. A burst of gunfire blew up a jar right next to them.

"Left! Go left!"

They turned, then turned again, and ran straight into a wall. A dead end.

The first one flattened himself against the stone.

"Shit, we're trapped! Give me the gun!"

The second one tossed him his submachine gun.

"Here, take it and spray anything that moves and wants you dead!"

He caught it in midair, dove behind a pile of crates and opened fire just as the Toride soldiers came around the corner. One soldier went down. The others threw themselves into cover.

"Contact! Dead end, ten o'clock!" a voice shouted. "They're cornered!"

The return fire came instantly. The crates exploded into splinters one by one.

"I'm almost out!" the first one yelled.

"I know, I know!"

The second one looked at the wall behind them, then at the mouth of the alley. The soldiers were advancing, covering one another.

"Okay… we're gonna have to improvise."

The shooting started up again, harder than before.

The first one rose behind the crates and emptied his magazine toward the mouth of the alley. A Toride soldier collapsed. Then another.

"Yeah! Come on, you dogs!"

But around the corner, more black helmets appeared. Four. Then six. Then ten.

"How many of them are there, damn it?!"

"Too many! Reload, reload!"

The second one tossed him a magazine. The first one slammed it in, raised the gun to his shoulder…

A bullet hit him square in the chest.

He took one step back and looked at the hole in his leather vest, as if he didn't understand. The gun slipped from his hands.

"No… no, no, no!"

The second one threw himself on him and dragged him behind what was left of the crates. He pressed both hands on the wound. The blood ran between his fingers, warm, far too fast.

"Stay with me! Stay with me, you hear me?!"

The first one opened his mouth. Nothing came out. His eyes stayed fixed on the blue sky of the Anarchy, then stopped moving.

The second one stayed still for a second. Just one.

"Cease fire!" a voice called from the Toride side. "There's one left! We want him alive!"

He picked up his partner's gun, held it tight against him and looked around. The wall behind. The soldiers in front. A broken window, two meters up, off to the side.

"Alive, huh…"

He fired a burst toward the mouth of the alley. The soldiers dove for cover. In the same second, he leapt onto a crate, grabbed the window ledge and hauled himself inside. Shards of glass sliced into his arms.

"He's going through the window! Surround the building!"

He landed in a dark room that smelled of dust and oil. He didn't stop. He crossed the hallway, tore down a staircase, smashed open a door with his shoulder. Behind him, boots were already climbing the stairs.

He ran, lungs on fire, the gun in one hand, the other pressed against his belt.

He could think of only one thing: getting back to Akasuna.

He kicked open a door.

A whole family was sitting at the table. The father, the mother, three kids, bowls of soup in their hands. Every head turned at the same time.

"Sorry!" he shouted as he crossed the room.

He knocked over a chair, jumped over the table and left through the back door. Behind him, the Toride soldiers burst into the kitchen.

"Which way did he go?!"

The father pointed his spoon at the back door, without even getting up.

The fugitive was already in the house next door. He charged down a hallway, turned and fired a blind burst behind him. A vase exploded, a painting fell, and a soldier hit the floor.

"He's shooting! He's shooting!"

"Of course he's shooting, move!"

Another door. Locked. He smashed it open with his shoulder and came face to face with an old man in his underwear, shaving in front of a mirror.

"Oh, is the gunfire for you again?" the old man sighed.

"Sorry, old timer!"

He opened the window, jumped onto the neighboring roof and landed heavily in a courtyard full of drying laundry. The sheets wrapped around him. He thrashed and swore, tore everything off and ran on, a white sheet still hanging from his shoulder.

Bullets rained down from the roof. The clotheslines snapped. A chicken took off screaming.

He turned, raised the gun and fired. The soldier on the roof pulled back into cover.

"He's in the courtyard! Cut off his exit!"

He crossed a carpet shop, knocking over two entire piles. He smashed through the back door, burst out into another alley and felt the magazine click empty.

Out of bullets.

He threw the gun away, pulled the pistol from his belt and started running again. In the distance, above the rooftops, the tall red towers of Akasuna were already in sight.

Three more streets.

Maybe four.

Behind him, the Toride boots weren't slowing down.

He reached the end of the last alley, and the city stopped all at once.

In front of him there was nothing but desert. Red dunes as far as the eye could see, and the sun crushing everything.

He didn't think. He ran.

His boots sank into the sand with every step. The sheet still hanging from his shoulder snapped in the hot wind. Behind him, the Toride soldiers were coming out of the city one after another.

"He's heading into the desert!"

"After him! Don't lose him!"

Five. Ten. Fifteen. Twenty black helmets advancing in a line across the sand, rifles raised.

He turned and fired two pistol rounds. Neither hit anyone. The soldiers didn't even bother to duck.

"Stop!" one of them shouted. "You won't get anywhere! There's nothing in this desert!"

"There's less of you, at least!" he yelled without slowing down.

He scrambled up a dune on all fours, the burning sand under his hands, and half rolled down the other side. He got up, spat out sand and kept going.

His legs were starting to shake. His throat was as dry as the desert itself. The blood from the cuts on his arms had dried into red crusts mixed with dust.

Behind him, the Toride soldiers weren't running. They were walking, at a steady pace, in formation. They didn't need to run.

The desert would end up stopping him for them.

"Come on… come on…" he panted, gripping his pistol. "Akasuna… it's not far… it's not far…"

He looked ahead. The red towers of Akasuna shimmered in the distance through the heat.

They didn't seem to be getting any closer.

He pushed his legs harder. Faster. Even faster.

The sand flew around him. His heart pounded so hard he could hear it in his ears. He wasn't looking back anymore. He was only looking at the red towers.

He didn't hear the footsteps closing in behind him.

A Toride soldier had broken away from the line. Younger, faster than the others, he had left his rifle with a colleague and run with everything he had too.

He leapt.

The impact threw the fugitive face first into the sand. The pistol flew out of his hand and slid a meter away. He thrashed, kicked, tried to turn over, but the soldier crushed his back with a knee and twisted his arm behind him.

"Don't move! Don't move!"

"Get off me! Get off me, you bastard!"

"It's over, buddy. It's over."

A metallic click. The cold of a handcuff around one wrist. Then the other.

The fugitive stopped moving. He lay there, cheek against the burning sand, out of breath, eyes fixed on the red towers of Akasuna.

They were still just as far away.

A second soldier came jogging up, bent down and picked the pistol up from the sand. He looked it over, emptied it and slipped the bullets into his pocket.

"Nice run," he said. "Really. We almost could've let you win."

The other eighteen were coming up behind, in no hurry.

The soldier who had tackled him pulled him up by the collar and forced him onto his knees. The fugitive spat out sand and looked up at them. Twenty black helmets. Twenty rifles. And the sun of the Anarchy above, giving no one any favors.

"So," the soldier said, wiping the sweat under his helmet. "You and me are gonna have a long talk."

The soldier raised a hand to his radio.

"This is unit three. Suspect apprehended. Requesting a vehicle at our position, we…"

He stopped.

At the top of the dune, facing them, silhouettes had just appeared. About ten. Red scarves, leather jackets, weapons in hand. On their armbands, the same drop of blood.

"Contact! Dune, twelve o'clock!"

The twenty Toride rifles rose in a single movement. The clan mercenaries didn't move. They weren't aiming at anyone. They were waiting.

Then, without a word, they stepped aside.

Someone was coming down the dune behind them.

He walked slowly, unhurried, as if the sand didn't bother him. A raised hood hid his face in shadow. A cape of black feathers covered his shoulders, and from his belt hung vials, pouches and a dagger. In his right hand he held a tall staff topped with a red orb that glowed faintly, like a beating heart.

The soldier holding the radio let it drop against his vest.

No one in unit three needed to be told who this was.

The man stopped a few meters from them. He glanced briefly at the prisoner kneeling in the sand, then raised his head toward the soldiers.

"You have no business here, soldier. This is my territory."

His voice was calm. Cold. Without anger.

The soldier in command of the unit took a step forward. His hand trembled slightly on the grip of his rifle, but his voice held.

"Your man stole, wrecked the place and killed a soldier. It would be worrying if we'd let him get away with that, don't you think?"

Crimson didn't answer right away.

The red orb pulsed once. Then a second time.

The soldier felt something strange. A throbbing in his temples, stronger than usual. A heat rising in his veins. Next to him, one of his men raised a hand to his nose. His fingers came back red.

"You will leave my territory," said Crimson, "or I will drain every drop of blood from your miserable carcass."

Silence fell over the desert.

Twenty rifles. About ten mercenaries. A single hooded man.

And yet, in unit three, everyone knew perfectly well which side had the advantage.

The soldier didn't take his eyes off Crimson. Slowly, very slowly, he raised the radio back to his mouth.

"Unit three to the Junta. Critical situation. The leader of the Chimamire clan is on site. I repeat, Crimson is on site. Requesting authorization to… to… Awaiting your orders."

Static.

Nothing.

The seconds stretched on. A drop of sweat ran down under the soldier's helmet. The prisoner, still on his knees, gave a little smile. Crimson didn't move a millimeter.

Then the radio crackled.

"Good day to you, chief of the Bandit Republic."

A deep voice, hoarse, calm. The voice of an old man who had seen too many battlefields to get worked up over the phone.

General Gérard Eldrath himself.

Crimson turned his head slightly toward the radio.

"General Gérard. I don't think you know who you're dealing with."

Behind the unit leader, a young soldier leaned toward the man next to him and whispered:

"The general's gonna send in the army. He won't be laughing then."

His neighbor didn't answer. Blood was still running from his nose.

The radio crackled again.

"Take back your man, Crimson, if you let my soldiers leave."

Total silence.

The young soldier opened his mouth, closed it, then opened it again.

"Wait… what?"

The unit leader turned to him with a look that clearly meant: shut up.

Crimson stood still for a long moment. Then the red orb of his staff stopped pulsing. The soldiers felt the heat leave their veins all at once, like a hand loosening its grip.

"Take off his handcuffs," Crimson said simply.

The soldier who had tackled the fugitive looked at his leader. His leader looked at the radio. The radio said nothing more.

"… Do what he says."

The clink of the handcuffs echoed in the silence of the desert. The prisoner got up rubbing his wrists, scraped a little dignity together from the sand and rejoined the clan mercenaries without looking back.

As he passed the young soldier, he gave him a wink.

"Nice run, huh?"

The Toride vehicle arrived a few minutes later, in a cloud of red dust.

No one spoke while the soldiers climbed aboard. The twenty black helmets crammed into the back, rifles between their knees, without taking their eyes off the dune where the Chimamire clan still stood.

The engine roared. The vehicle turned around and drove off toward the border.

In the back, the young soldier couldn't hold it in anymore.

"I don't get it."

"Shut up," his neighbor muttered, a blood-soaked handkerchief under his nose.

"No, seriously. That's Crimson. The most wanted criminal in the world. He was right there, five meters from us, and the general… he just lets him go? Like that?"

"Did you see what he did to us without even moving? What did you want, for us to shoot him?"

"I don't know! Send in the army! Tanks! A bomb! Anything!"

The unit leader, sitting up front, didn't turn around.

"The general made his decision," he said. "He saved twenty lives today. Period."

The young soldier opened his mouth, then closed it. Through the rear window he watched the clan silhouettes shrinking at the top of the dune.

"Still," he muttered. "It's weird."

No one answered him.

On the dune, Crimson watched the vehicle disappear over the horizon. He stayed still until the sound of the engine had completely died away.

The clan member who had just been freed came over, head down.

"Boss… thank you. I…"

"Your partner is dead."

It wasn't a question. The fugitive lowered his head even further.

"Yes, boss."

Crimson said nothing more. He turned and began to climb back up the dune, staff in hand, his cape of black feathers quivering in the hot wind. The mercenaries followed him without a word.

Behind them, the wind was already erasing the footprints in the sand.

"Left! Go left!" They turned, then turned again, and ran straight into a wall. A dead end. The first one flattened himself against the stone. "Shit, we're trapped! Give me the gun!" The second one tossed him his submachine gun. "Here, take it and spray anything that moves and wants you dead!" He caught it in midair, dove behind a pile of crates and opened fire just as the Toride soldiers came around the corner. One soldier went down. The others threw themselves into cover. "Contact! Dead end, ten o'clock!" a voice shouted. "They're cornered!" The return fire came instantly. The crates exploded into splinters one by one. "I'm almost out!" the first one yelled. "I know, I know!" The second one looked at the wall behind them, then at the mouth of the alley. The soldiers were advancing, covering one another. "Okay… we're gonna have to improvise." The shooting started up again, harder than before. The first one rose behind the crates and emptied his magazine toward the mouth of the alley. A Toride soldier collapsed. Then another. "Yeah! Come on, you dogs!" But around the corner, more black helmets appeared. Four. Then six. Then ten. "How many of them are there, damn it?!" "Too many! Reload, reload!" The second one tossed him a magazine. The first one slammed it in, raised the gun to his shoulder… A bullet hit him square in the chest. He took one step back and looked at the hole in his leather vest, as if he didn't understand. The gun slipped from his hands. "No… no, no, no!" The second one threw himself on him and dragged him behind what was left of the crates. He pressed both hands on the wound. The blood ran between his fingers, warm, far too fast. "Stay with me! Stay with me, you hear me?!" The first one opened his mouth. Nothing came out. His eyes stayed fixed on the blue sky of the Anarchy, then stopped moving. The second one stayed still for a second. Just one. "Cease fire!" a voice called from the Toride side. "There's one left! We want him alive!" He picked up his partner's gun, held it tight against him and looked around. The wall behind. The soldiers in front. A broken window, two meters up, off to the side. "Alive, huh…" He fired a burst toward the mouth of the alley. The soldiers dove for cover. In the same second, he leapt onto a crate, grabbed the window ledge and hauled himself inside. Shards of glass sliced into his arms. "He's going through the window! Surround the building!" He landed in a dark room that smelled of dust and oil. He didn't stop. He crossed the hallway, tore down a staircase, smashed open a door with his shoulder. Behind him, boots were already climbing the stairs. He ran, lungs on fire, the gun in one hand, the other pressed against his belt. He could think of only one thing: getting back to Akasuna. He kicked open a door. A whole family was sitting at the table. The father, the mother, three kids, bowls of soup in their hands. Every head turned at the same time. "Sorry!" he shouted as he crossed the room. He knocked over a chair, jumped over the table and left through the back door. Behind him, the Toride soldiers burst into the kitchen. "Which way did he go?!" The father pointed his spoon at the back door, without even getting up. The fugitive was already in the house next door. He charged down a hallway, turned and fired a blind burst behind him. A vase exploded, a painting fell, and a soldier hit the floor. "He's shooting! He's shooting!" "Of course he's shooting, move!" Another door. Locked. He smashed it open with his shoulder and came face to face with an old man in his underwear, shaving in front of a mirror. "Oh, is the gunfire for you again?" the old man sighed. "Sorry, old timer!" He opened the window, jumped onto the neighboring roof and landed heavily in a courtyard full of drying laundry. The sheets wrapped around him. He thrashed and swore, tore everything off and ran on, a white sheet still hanging from his shoulder. Bullets rained down from the roof. The clotheslines snapped. A chicken took off screaming. He turned, raised the gun and fired. The soldier on the roof pulled back into cover. "He's in the courtyard! Cut off his exit!" He crossed a carpet shop, knocking over two entire piles. He smashed through the back door, burst out into another alley and felt the magazine click empty. Out of bullets. He threw the gun away, pulled the pistol from his belt and started running again. In the distance, above the rooftops, the tall red towers of Akasuna were already in sight. Three more streets. Maybe four. Behind him, the Toride boots weren't slowing down. He reached the end of the last alley, and the city stopped all at once. In front of him there was nothing but desert. Red dunes as far as the eye could see, and the sun crushing everything. He didn't think. He ran. His boots sank into the sand with every step. The sheet still hanging from his shoulder snapped in the hot wind. Behind him, the Toride soldiers were coming out of the city one after another. "He's heading into the desert!" "After him! Don't lose him!" Five. Ten. Fifteen. Twenty black helmets advancing in a line across the sand, rifles raised. He turned and fired two pistol rounds. Neither hit anyone. The soldiers didn't even bother to duck. "Stop!" one of them shouted. "You won't get anywhere! There's nothing in this desert!" "There's less of you, at least!" he yelled without slowing down. He scrambled up a dune on all fours, the burning sand under his hands, and half rolled down the other side. He got up, spat out sand and kept going. His legs were starting to shake. His throat was as dry as the desert itself. The blood from the cuts on his arms had dried into red crusts mixed with dust. Behind him, the Toride soldiers weren't running. They were walking, at a steady pace, in formation. They didn't need to run. The desert would end up stopping him for them. "Come on… come on…" he panted, gripping his pistol. "Akasuna… it's not far… it's not far…" He looked ahead. The red towers of Akasuna shimmered in the distance through the heat. They didn't seem to be getting any closer. He pushed his legs harder. Faster. Even faster. The sand flew around him. His heart pounded so hard he could hear it in his ears. He wasn't looking back anymore. He was only looking at the red towers. He didn't hear the footsteps closing in behind him. A Toride soldier had broken away from the line. Younger, faster than the others, he had left his rifle with a colleague and run with everything he had too. He leapt. The impact threw the fugitive face first into the sand. The pistol flew out of his hand and slid a meter away. He thrashed, kicked, tried to turn over, but the soldier crushed his back with a knee and twisted his arm behind him. "Don't move! Don't move!" "Get off me! Get off me, you bastard!" "It's over, buddy. It's over." A metallic click. The cold of a handcuff around one wrist. Then the other. The fugitive stopped moving. He lay there, cheek against the burning sand, out of breath, eyes fixed on the red towers of Akasuna. They were still just as far away. A second soldier came jogging up, bent down and picked the pistol up from the sand. He looked it over, emptied it and slipped the bullets into his pocket. "Nice run," he said. "Really. We almost could've let you win." The other eighteen were coming up behind, in no hurry. The soldier who had tackled him pulled him up by the collar and forced him onto his knees. The fugitive spat out sand and looked up at them. Twenty black helmets. Twenty rifles. And the sun of the Anarchy above, giving no one any favors. "So," the soldier said, wiping the sweat under his helmet. "You and me are gonna have a long talk." The soldier raised a hand to his radio. "This is unit three. Suspect apprehended. Requesting a vehicle at our position, we…" He stopped. At the top of the dune, facing them, silhouettes had just appeared. About ten. Red scarves, leather jackets, weapons in hand. On their armbands, the same drop of blood. "Contact! Dune, twelve o'clock!" The twenty Toride rifles rose in a single movement. The clan mercenaries didn't move. They weren't aiming at anyone. They were waiting. Then, without a word, they stepped aside. Someone was coming down the dune behind them. He walked slowly, unhurried, as if the sand didn't bother him. A raised hood hid his face in shadow. A cape of black feathers covered his shoulders, and from his belt hung vials, pouches and a dagger. In his right hand he held a tall staff topped with a red orb that glowed faintly, like a beating heart. The soldier holding the radio let it drop against his vest. No one in unit three needed to be told who this was. The man stopped a few meters from them. He glanced briefly at the prisoner kneeling in the sand, then raised his head toward the soldiers. "You have no business here, soldier. This is my territory." His voice was calm. Cold. Without anger. The soldier in command of the unit took a step forward. His hand trembled slightly on the grip of his rifle, but his voice held. "Your man stole, wrecked the place and killed a soldier. It would be worrying if we'd let him get away with that, don't you think?" Crimson didn't answer right away. The red orb pulsed once. Then a second time. The soldier felt something strange. A throbbing in his temples, stronger than usual. A heat rising in his veins. Next to him, one of his men raised a hand to his nose. His fingers came back red. "You will leave my territory," said Crimson, "or I will drain every drop of blood from your miserable carcass." Silence fell over the desert. Twenty rifles. About ten mercenaries. A single hooded man. And yet, in unit three, everyone knew perfectly well which side had the advantage. The soldier didn't take his eyes off Crimson. Slowly, very slowly, he raised the radio back to his mouth. "Unit three to the Junta. Critical situation. The leader of the Chimamire clan is on site. I repeat, Crimson is on site. Requesting authorization to… to… Awaiting your orders." Static. Nothing. The seconds stretched on. A drop of sweat ran down under the soldier's helmet. The prisoner, still on his knees, gave a little smile. Crimson didn't move a millimeter. Then the radio crackled. "Good day to you, chief of the Bandit Republic." A deep voice, hoarse, calm. The voice of an old man who had seen too many battlefields to get worked up over the phone. General Gérard Eldrath himself. Crimson turned his head slightly toward the radio. "General Gérard. I don't think you know who you're dealing with." Behind the unit leader, a young soldier leaned toward the man next to him and whispered: "The general's gonna send in the army. He won't be laughing then." His neighbor didn't answer. Blood was still running from his nose. The radio crackled again. "Take back your man, Crimson, if you let my soldiers leave." Total silence. The young soldier opened his mouth, closed it, then opened it again. "Wait… what?" The unit leader turned to him with a look that clearly meant: shut up . Crimson stood still for a long moment. Then the red orb of his staff stopped pulsing. The soldiers felt the heat leave their veins all at once, like a hand loosening its grip. "Take off his handcuffs," Crimson said simply. The soldier who had tackled the fugitive looked at his leader. His leader looked at the radio. The radio said nothing more. "… Do what he says." The clink of the handcuffs echoed in the silence of the desert. The prisoner got up rubbing his wrists, scraped a little dignity together from the sand and rejoined the clan mercenaries without looking back. As he passed the young soldier, he gave him a wink. "Nice run, huh?" The Toride vehicle arrived a few minutes later, in a cloud of red dust. No one spoke while the soldiers climbed aboard. The twenty black helmets crammed into the back, rifles between their knees, without taking their eyes off the dune where the Chimamire clan still stood. The engine roared. The vehicle turned around and drove off toward the border. In the back, the young soldier couldn't hold it in anymore. "I don't get it." "Shut up," his neighbor muttered, a blood-soaked handkerchief under his nose. "No, seriously. That's Crimson. The most wanted criminal in the world. He was right there, five meters from us, and the general… he just lets him go? Like that?" "Did you see what he did to us without even moving? What did you want, for us to shoot him?" "I don't know! Send in the army! Tanks! A bomb! Anything!" The unit leader, sitting up front, didn't turn around. "The general made his decision," he said. "He saved twenty lives today. Period." The young soldier opened his mouth, then closed it. Through the rear window he watched the clan silhouettes shrinking at the top of the dune. "Still," he muttered. "It's weird." No one answered him. On the dune, Crimson watched the vehicle disappear over the horizon. He stayed still until the sound of the engine had completely died away. The clan member who had just been freed came over, head down. "Boss… thank you. I…" "Your partner is dead." It wasn't a question. The fugitive lowered his head even further. "Yes, boss." Crimson said nothing more. He turned and began to climb back up the dune, staff in hand, his cape of black feathers quivering in the hot wind. The mercenaries followed him without a word. Behind them, the wind was already erasing the footprints in the sand.
